name: social-row
description:
The row of social marks beside the wordmark in the header, and again in the footer. Four links, icon-only, quiet until pointed at.

A unit because it is the same row twice with two different inks — dark on the header's pale bar, light on the footer's marine ground — and because the thing that keeps going wrong with it is not the look. An icon-only link has no accessible name unless someone gives it one, and a row of four is four unnamed links: a screen reader reads "link, link, link, link". Both existing copies pass an `aria-label` per item, which is correct and is exactly the care that gets dropped on the fifth copy.

It takes its ink from `currentColor`, so a surface tints the ROW once and every mark follows. The header does this today by passing a different class per context.
surfaceNote: the profile row in the bar and the menu

base.$description:
A row that never wraps and never grows. In a header it sits between the wordmark and the nav, and a social row that wraps to a second line pushes the bar's height around on exactly the widths where space is tightest.

Not a container: `fit-content` is width from contents, which containment removes.

IT DECLARES `--icon-tint`, the colour the engine paints a duotone's secondary layer with. Declared HERE, on the unit that draws the glyph, and not once at the document root: a global custom property is the anti-pattern the whole scoping design exists to avoid — two brands on one page write the same name and the second wins. An app shell is no better, because a shell is a container that may host more than one vibe. A unit is the smallest thing that owns its own subtree, so the tint travels with the component that needs it and reaches nothing else.

item.$description: One mark. `currentColor` throughout, so the ROW is tinted once and every icon follows — the alternative is a colour per mark and four places to forget. The target is padded to 24px against an 18px glyph: WCAG 2.5.8 measures the TARGET, not the drawing, and four adjacent 18px links are four near-misses in a row.

density.$description: How much air between the marks.

tight.$description: For a header already carrying a nav and a call to action.

reducedMotion.$description: The fade stays as an instant change. Hover here is a courtesy, not information, so there is nothing to lose by making it immediate.

a11y.note:
`role="group"` with a label, NOT `role="list"`.

It was a list, and it was a broken one: `role="list"` obliges an element to contain `listitem` children, and the marks sit one level down inside the `items` wrapper that does the layout. axe-core calls that CRITICAL (`aria-required-children`), and it is right — a list that announces no items is worse than no list, because a screen-reader user is told to expect a structure that is not there.

Making it a real list would mean `ul`/`li` around every link, which is markup added to satisfy a role rather than to describe anything: four links to four profiles are not an ordered set and nothing depends on their count. A labelled group says exactly what this is.

Every mark needs its own accessible name — an `aria-label` naming the NETWORK, not the icon: "avenCEO on LinkedIn", never "LinkedIn logo". The glyph is `aria-hidden`, because an icon announced beside a labelled link is the name read twice.

The row is `role="list"` with a label, so a screen reader can skip it as a unit rather than walking four links to discover they were all social.

Off-site links open in a new tab in both existing copies, which needs `rel="noopener noreferrer"` — and a link that changes context without warning is WCAG 3.2.5, so the name should say so.

The target is 24px against an 18px glyph, measured on the target, which is what 2.5.8 counts.
